Behaviour
be-have'yur
n. (outward conduct and bearing; a qualification for the eldership, a standard for aged women, and the thing David changed before Achish)
From behave — be- intensive plus have, in the old sense of bearing or holding oneself. The Greek at 1 Timothy 3:2 is kosmios, orderly and well-arranged, from kosmos, order; at Titus 2:3 it is katastema, demeanour or deportment.

Biblical Definition

Paul makes outward bearing a formal qualification for office: “A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach” (1 Timothy 3:2). The Greek kosmios is the adjective of kosmos, order — the same word behind the universe as an ordered whole. An elder's life is to be arranged rather than chaotic, and the requirement stands in a list of things any congregation can actually observe. Titus applies the parallel standard to older women: “The aged women likewise, that they be in behaviour as becometh holiness, not false accusers, not given to much wine, teachers of good things” (Titus 2:3), where katastema means settled demeanour — the bearing a person has when nothing in particular is happening. Against these stands a strange episode: fleeing Saul and recognised in Gath, “he changed his behaviour before them, and feigned himself mad in their hands, and scrabbled on the doors of the gate, and let his spittle fall down upon his beard” (1 Samuel 21:13). The psalm David wrote about that day begins “I will bless the LORD at all times” (Psalm 34:1).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines behavior as manner of behaving, conduct, deportment, and course of life with respect to morals.

expand to see more

BEHAVIOR, n. Manner of behaving, whether good or bad; conduct; manners; carriage of one's self, with respect to propriety or morals; deportment.

It expresses external appearance or action; sometimes in a particular character; more generally in the common duties of life.

2. Conduct; course of life.

To be upon one's behavior, is to be in a state of trial, in which something important depends on propriety of conduct.

BEHAVE, v.t. To restrain; to govern; to subdue.

Key Scripture

1 Timothy 3:2 — "A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach;"

Titus 2:3 — "The aged women likewise, that they be in behaviour as becometh holiness, not false accusers, not given to much wine, teachers of good things;"

1 Samuel 21:13 — "And he changed his behaviour before them, and feigned himself mad in their hands, and scrabbled on the doors of the gate, and let his spittle fall down upon his beard."

Psalm 34:1 — "A Psalm of David, when he changed his behaviour before Abimelech; who drove him away, and he departed. I will bless the LORD at all times: his praise shall continually be in my mouth."

Modern Corruption

Character is now assessed by declared belief and stated intention, and Paul assesses it by observable conduct that a congregation can check.

expand to see more

The modern instinct is that the inner life is the real person and outward conduct is a performance that may or may not represent it — so a man is judged by what he affirms and how he understands himself. Paul's qualification lists work the other way. Every item in 1 Timothy 3 is externally verifiable: whether he is the husband of one wife, whether he is given to wine, whether he is a striker, whether his children are in subjection, whether he has a good report of them which are without. Of good behaviour belongs to that list, and it is there because a church calling a man to office is not equipped to read his heart and is entirely equipped to watch his life.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself. The principle to recover is the New Testament's confidence in observable conduct, and its patience. Titus 2:3 uses katastema, settled demeanour, and pairs it with a positive charge — aged women are to be teachers of good things, that they may teach the young women. The passage assumes a congregation in which generations are in contact and the older are watched by the younger. That structure is where behaviour becomes instruction, and it cannot be replaced by a curriculum. David's morning in Gath is a reminder that even a man after God's own heart had days he had to write a psalm about afterward.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek kosmios, orderly — 1 Timothy 3:2; kosmos, order, the universe; katastema, demeanour — Titus 2:3; Hebrew taam, taste or discretion — 1 Samuel 21:13.

expand to see more

Greek kosmios — orderly, well arranged; 1 Timothy 3:2, and of women's apparel in 2:9.

Greek kosmos — order, arrangement, and so the ordered universe; the root of kosmios.

Greek katastema — settled demeanour, deportment; Titus 2:3, its only New Testament occurrence.

Greek hieroprepes — as becometh holiness, priestly in bearing; the standard set in the same verse.

Hebrew taam — taste, judgment, discretion; 1 Samuel 21:13, what David changed.

Usage

"“Of good behaviour” — kosmios, a life arranged rather than chaotic."

"“In behaviour as becometh holiness” — settled demeanour, and then teaching."

"“He changed his behaviour before them” — and wrote Psalm 34 about the day."
